prize_parts.citation: for foundational contributions to the analysis of nominal rigidities and monetary policy: time-dependent price setting, staggered contracts and policy rules, and a micro-founded theory of interest-rate policy

statement.case_for: My preferred part is unchanged from round 1: B014 with Calvo, Taylor and Woodford. After the exchange I hold it for three reasons. (1) The three credited contributions are separable and each can be traced to a specific body of work: the tractable pricing friction, staggered contracts with the policy rule, and the welfare-based synthesis of interest and prices. (2) The work is 25 to 40 years old. It has been used for policy analysis and revised after the zero lower bound, 2008 and 2021-23, not dropped. (3) The earlier macro prizes cover expectations, time consistency, identification and banking crises, and none recognised the nominal-rigidity and policy-rule core. I read my own field's lens into this. I care about what an estimate identifies, and the citation I propose credits mechanisms and a way of reasoning about policy. It does not credit settled structural parameter values or the forecasting record of any one model. On Calvo versus Galí, my labour-economics experience of structural estimation adds a small point to the pricing-primitive argument. Estimated New Keynesian Phillips-curve coefficients depend heavily on identifying assumptions, so Galí's empirical strand is the part most exposed to debate, while the pricing device is the part that is not. That is background knowledge, not verified here. I would not call Galí a weaker claimant. I move him to the strongest omitted name, and I would accept the swap only if the committee decides the citation should be weighted to the estimated framework. I change one alternative: B047 replaces B018 as my second alternative. Nobody preferred B018 in round 1, and the contested wealth and offshore measurement and the r > g reading are unresolved. B047 has two supporters, more than twenty years of firm-level testing, and a stable two-name attribution. My list of alternatives is not a ranking by support counts. It records which cases I would accept if B014's attribution problem proved unsolvable.
statement.case_against: Attribution remains the main weakness and the cap of three names cannot remove it. Christiano, Eichenbaum and Evans, Smets and Wouters, Galí and Gertler all made contributions that made the framework usable and testable, and any wording that names three risks being read as ranking them below. Calvo's pricing device is compact, and it is fair to ask whether it is a discovery in the sense the committee normally rewards, or a modelling convenience whose significance comes from what was built on it. The representative-agent form of the framework is widely seen as being superseded by heterogeneous-agent models, so the prize could be read as honouring a stage of development. The 2008 and 2021-23 performance questions are not settled. Finally, B003 has a cleaner and undisputed attribution, and I take that as a real point in its favour rather than a drafting detail. I have not independently verified any priority claim.

responses.point: Strömberg prefers B003 (Kiyotaki and Moore, dropping Gertler). He concedes B014 has the larger footprint in practice and says he would support B014 if a defensible narrower citation were found, but that otherwise B003 is the cleaner prize.
responses.response: I think the narrower citation can be written. It names three mechanisms instead of a broad framework: time-dependent price setting, staggered contracts and policy rules, and the micro-founded theory of interest-rate policy. It makes no claim about the estimated medium-scale DSGE tradition, and it does not say that this is the whole framework. That does not eliminate the omission problem, but it states what is credited and leaves the rest open. I agree with you on the 2022 overlap. Kiyotaki-Moore is about borrowers' collateral and asset-price amplification, which differs from the intermediation and crisis-history work, so I would not weigh overlap against B003. For me B014 goes ahead on breadth of influence over how policy is analysed and communicated. Another reason is that its mechanisms have been confronted with data and extended more often than the single 1997 theory paper behind B003, whose empirical support came mostly from later work. I regard the gap as modest, not large. B003 stays my first alternative. If you consider the citation as drafted still implies a ranking against omitted contributors, I would like to hear that objection specifically.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson also holds Calvo, Taylor and Woodford, and in her response to my opening trio says that Galí in place of Calvo is the natural swap if the committee weights empirical validation and the estimated-model tradition more heavily. She would not object strongly to that swap.
responses.response: I agree with the conditional and with where the line falls. If the citation were rebuilt around the empirical framework, Galí would replace Calvo. I do not think that is the right citation, because the empirical record of the framework is the contested part, and estimates depend on identifying assumptions that deserve more scepticism than the mechanism. My own opening trio included Galí, and I changed it because the ballot item is defined by nominal rigidities and the pricing friction is the primitive. We differ little. The test I would use is whether the citation can survive a weak empirical result. The Calvo-Taylor-Woodford wording does, and a Galí-weighted wording would be exposed to every subsequent reassessment of Phillips-curve estimates.

responses.point: Krusell holds Calvo, Taylor and Woodford as three distinct conceptual steps. He accepts the cost of excluding Galí, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets, and notes that representative-agent versions are widely seen as superseded by heterogeneous-agent models, which are his own field.
responses.response: I take the superseded point seriously, and your field makes you the best-placed member to say it. I read it differently: that heterogeneous-agent work extends or criticises this baseline is itself the sign of a foundational contribution. The citation should not claim that representative-agent models are the end state. That is another reason to credit mechanisms (pricing friction, rule, synthesis) and not a particular model class. Where I would press you is the estimated-DSGE strand. You list its exclusion as a cost, and I would like that cost named openly in the committee's deliberation. I would not accept a justification that treats Christiano-Eichenbaum-Evans or Smets-Wouters as derivative. Andersson is right that their work on identifying monetary shocks is a different kind of contribution, not a lesser one. I note that you and I share an institutional overlap at Stockholm (2010-17), and I try not to count agreement from you as evidence.

responses.point: Boppart prefers B047 (Melitz and Helpman) because it has the cleanest attribution and more than twenty years of firm-level confirmation. He ranks B014 second because any trio is contestable on attribution, and says the choice of what to credit (older contract and rule insights versus the modern synthesis) is unresolved.
responses.response: Your last point is the right one, and I answer it directly. The citation credits the older contract and rule insights and the modern synthesis together, as three separable parts, and says so. That is a defined scope. On B047 I agree the attribution is cleaner and that Melitz is the clear originator, so it is now my second alternative. I weigh the Krugman overlap and the Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum priority questions as costs that a careful citation can reduce but not remove, since those names would stay outside the award. You are right that attribution cleanliness and impact are different, and I do not think a tidier credit list settles the ordering by itself. I also agree that the years since 2008 are not merit.

responses.point: Dreber agrees on B014 and treats the third name (Calvo or Galí) as the key open question. In her round-1 response on B018 she would restrict credit to Piketty and Saez because wealth and offshore estimates are contested, and she would add Zucman only for a settled strand.
responses.response: I accept your B018 reasoning and it contributes to my dropping B018 as an alternative. A top-incomes series is a durable public good, but the wealth-allocation methods are still contested and a pair would leave out a co-author of much of the wealth work. In the proposal that is a different award from the one I listed. On the Calvo-versus-Galí question we end up at the same place: Calvo is the more clearly originating contribution, and Galí is the strongest omitted claim. I would add that your point about durability as a criterion applies to the mechanism, not to the estimated model.

uncertainties: Whether any three-name B014 citation can avoid implying a ranking against Christiano, Eichenbaum, Evans, Smets, Wouters, Galí and Gertler. My wording limits what is credited but may not fully remove the implication.

Whether Calvo's pricing device is judged a discovery in the sense the committee usually rewards, and whether Galí should replace him if the committee favours a citation weighted to the empirical framework.

How much room the 2022 prize and earlier macro prizes leave, and how the post-2021 inflation and the heterogeneous-agent critique bear on maturity. I regard these as extensions of the framework, but the committee has not settled the matter.
Whether Strömberg's and Teorell's conditional support for B014 would hold with the narrower wording. I cannot determine that from the files.
Whether the B014 versus B003 ordering should turn on breadth of practical influence, as I think, or on cleaner attribution and no disputed names, which are the reasons for B003.
I rely on background knowledge for priority, attribution and the empirical standing of Phillips-curve estimates. I have not independently verified any of it from the supplied evidence.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. My profile lists no co-authorship or institutional link to Calvo, Taylor or Woodford, nor to the other B014 names, to Kiyotaki and Moore (B003), or to Melitz and Helpman (B047). My co-authors are in the Uppsala and IFAU labour-economics network (including Bertil Holmlund, who is also a frequent co-author of Hjalmarsson) and none is a candidate. I overlapped with the IIES macro group (Hassler, Krusell) at Stockholm University in 2010-17 without co-authoring; both are committee colleagues and not candidates, and I have tried not to treat their agreement as merit. My presentation speeches as chair, including 2021, may reflect collective drafting and do not indicate a preference here. Disclosed, not adjudicated.
